title: Universally closed morphisms of algebraic spaces are quasi-compact
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] and let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$ [def-trf-algebraic-space], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Use sheaf fibre products [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers] and the atlas topology on point spaces [def-a1-space-point-topology]. Suppose $f$ is universally closed: for every algebraic space $Y'$ over $S$ and morphism $Y'\to Y$, the induced map $|X\times_Y Y'|\to|Y'|$ is closed [def-sfb-space-morphism-properties]. Then $f$ is quasi-compact: for every affine scheme $T\to Y$, the point space $|X\times_YT|$ is quasi-compact, meaning that every open covering has a finite subcover. Here an affine scheme is a scheme isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. No representability, separatedness, finite-type or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: Fix an affine scheme $Y_0\to Y$ and put $X_0=X\times_YY_0$. For every $T\to Y_0$, the fibre-product universal property identifies $X_0\times_{Y_0}T$ with $X\times_YT$. Universal closedness of $f$ therefore gives universal closedness of $X_0\to Y_0$ directly from its definition. It suffices to prove that $|X_0|$ is quasi-compact for each such test. Rename $X_0,Y_0$ as $X,Y$, write $Y=\operatorname{Spec}B$, and suppose for contradiction that $|X|$ is not quasi-compact.

Choose a set-indexed Zariski covering $X=\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i$ whose members admit surjective etale maps from affine schemes. Affine schemes are quasi-compact, and the atlas criterion for quasi-compactness makes each $|X_i|$ quasi-compact. Since the affine scheme $Y$ is quasi-separated, quasi-compact/quasi-separated permanence makes each morphism $X_i\to Y$ quasi-compact. Thus for every principal affine open $V\subset Y$, the point space of $X_{i,V}=X_i\times_YV$ is quasi-compact. These pullbacks are the inverse-image open subspaces by point-open calculus.

There is a point $y\in Y$ for which $|X_V|$ is not quasi-compact for every principal open neighbourhood $V=D(b)$ of $y$. Otherwise choose such a neighbourhood with quasi-compact inverse image at every point. Quasi-compactness of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ selects finitely many covering $Y$. Their inverse images cover $X$, and a finite union of quasi-compact subsets is quasi-compact: restrict any open cover to each subset and unite the finitely many finite subcovers. This contradicts the choice of $X$. Fix this $y$.

Form the polynomial ring $A=B[a_i:i\in I]$, the affine scheme $T=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and $T_i=D(a_i)\subset T$. Write $P=T\times_YX$, with projections $p:P\to T$ and $q:P\to X$. Define the subset
$$C=|P|\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}\bigl(|p|^{-1}(T_i)\cap|q|^{-1}(|X_i|)\bigr).$$
The two point maps are continuous and the displayed subsets are open, so $C$ is closed. Universal closedness says $F=|p|(C)$ is closed in $T$. This uses a closed subset only; no reduced closed subspace structure is needed.

Let $t\in T$ be the point given by the ring map $A\to\kappa(y)$ taking coefficients through $B\to\kappa(y)$ and every $a_i$ to $1$; its kernel contracts to the prime $y$, and $t\in T_i$ for every $i$. If $z\in C$ mapped to $t$, choose $i$ with $q(z)\in|X_i|$. Then $p(z)\in T_i$ and $q(z)\in|X_i|$, contrary to the definition of $C$. Hence $t\notin F$. Since principal opens form a basis, choose $g\in A$ such that $t\in D(g)\subset T\setminus F$; equivalently $F\subset V(g)$ and $g(t)\ne0$.

The polynomial $g$ involves only finitely many variables; let $J\subset I$ contain all their indices. At least one coefficient $c\in B$ of $g$ has nonzero image in $\kappa(y)$, since otherwise evaluation of $g$ at $t$ would vanish. Put $V=D(c)$, a principal affine neighbourhood of $y$. The open subspaces $X_{j,V}$ for $j\in J$ cannot cover $X_V$: each is quasi-compact by step 2, whereas $|X_V|$ is not quasi-compact by step 3, and a finite union would be quasi-compact. Choose $x\in|X_V|\setminus\bigcup_{j\in J}|X_{j,V}|$ and put $v=f(x)\in V$. Thus $x\notin|X_j|$ for all $j\in J$.

Put $R=\kappa(v)[u_j:j\in J]$. This is an integral domain. Its zero ideal is prime; its residue field $L=\kappa_R((0))$ receives an injective map $R\hookrightarrow L$. Define $A	o L$ by $B	o\kappa(v)	o L$, $a_j\mapsto u_j$ for $j\in J$, and $a_i\mapsto0$ for $i
otin J$. The coefficient $c$ chosen in step 6 stays nonzero at $v$, so the image of $g$ is a nonzero polynomial in $R$, hence nonzero in $L$. The kernel defines a point $t'\in T$ above $v$ with $g
otin t'$ and $a_i\in t'$ for every $i
otin J$. This construction includes $J=\varnothing$ and works over finite residue fields; no assertion about rational values of a polynomial is used.

The points $x\in|X|$ and $t'\in|T|$ have the same image $v\in|Y|$. Surjectivity of the map from points of a fibre product to the fibre product of point sets gives $z\in|P|$ with $q(z)=x$ and $p(z)=t'$. For $j\in J$ we have $q(z)
otin|X_j|$; for $i
otin J$ we have $p(z)
otin D(a_i)$. Thus $z$ belongs to none of the open subsets removed in the definition of $C$, so $z\in C$. Consequently $t'\in F\subset V(g)$, contradicting $g
otin t'$. This contradiction proves $|X|$ quasi-compact. Step 1 applied to every affine test proves precisely the stated quasi-compactness of the original $f$.
